### I. The Salt on the Glass

At the far western spit of the peninsula, where the estuary of the Ouaniche gives way to the grey, uncreased swell of the northern shelf, stands the station. It has possessed four official names under three distinct hydrographic administrations, but in the logbooks that sit stacked in the lower scullery—bound in pigskin and warped into stiff, concave smiles by eighty years of damp—it is simply called *The Point*.

The building is made of dressed ballast-stone, basalt dark as wet liver, hauled out of the holds of empty colliers before the channel silted over. Above the stone sits an octagonal lantern room, though it has not held an open burner since the year of the hard frost, when the kerosene congealed in its copper leads like mutton fat. Now, the lantern houses instruments: thirty-two varieties of dial, vane, bob, and siphon, their brass limbs dulled by salt-scud to the color of dry moss.

My work here is neither military nor strictly scientific, though the ministry pays my quarterly stipend in crisp, indigo notes that arrive inside oilcloth pouches aboard the cutter *Phoebe*. In the ledger of the Treasury, I am listed as *Conservator of Terrestrial Constants (Retired Grade)*. It is a title that implies the universe is a house prone to settling, and that someone must go through the rooms with a boxwood level and a pocketful of cedar wedges to ensure the doors do not swing open of their own accord.

Every morning begins the same way: with a piece of flannel, four drops of rectified spirit, and the eastern face of the lantern glass.

The salt does not arrive as spray. It travels as a suspension, an aerosol so fine that it drifts inland through the keyholes and coats the spoons in the drawer. If left for forty-eight hours, it blooms into crusts that look like frost under a jeweler’s loupe—little hexagonal fortresses that bite into the crown glass and leave permanent pockmarks. To clean them requires a circular stroke, firm but without haste, starting from the center of each pane and spiraling toward the lead came.

While I rub, the sea below goes from charcoal to tin, then from tin to a yellow like the rind of a winter gourd. There are no gulls this late in October. There are only gannets, dropping like plumb-bobs into the tide-rips two miles out, and the silence of three hundred square leagues of water sliding over flat shale.

When the glass is clean, I turn to the tables.

***

### II. The Taxonomy of Obsolete Measures

Modern men believe that a meter is a meter everywhere, guaranteed by a piece of platinum-iridium kept under three nested bell-jars in a subterranean vault in Sèvres. They believe that an hour is an unvarying dividend of planetary rotation, chopped into equal ribbons by the chatter of quartz crystals.

They are mistaken, of course.

Before the harmonization of standards in the late seventies of the last century, measurement was local, physical, and tragic. It partook of the weather and the length of the parish priest’s ulna. In the high valleys of the Cantal, hay was sold by the *fourchée*, which was as much dried grass as a man of forty could lift on an ash fork without his heart hammering through his waistcoat. On the coast of Kerry, distance at sea was reckoned in *hearings*—the distance over which a bull’s roar could be distinguished above the break of the surf on an overcast afternoon.

The collection at the Point preserves the instruments that were abandoned when the world decided that everything should be exchangeable for everything else.

On the south bench rests the *Psychrometer of Mortifications*, built in 1842 by a clockmaker from Basel who believed that atmospheric moisture was not merely evaporated water, but the physical residue of human sighs. It consists of two mercury thermometers mounted on an ivory backplate. The wet bulb is wrapped not in cotton gauze, but in a strip of cambric torn from the shroud of a child who died of croup. It is an absurd device, mechanically speaking. Its readings fluctuate wildly whenever a fog bank rolls over the rocks, indicating an intolerable surplus of grief in the lower troposphere. Yet when one sits beside it during a gale, listening to the spruce rafters groan in their mortises, it is difficult not to look at the rising column of red spirit and feel that the Swiss mechanic was merely guilty of an excess of precision.

Beside it sits the *Vane of Uncertain Allegiance*. It is an iron arrow counterweighted by a hollow copper swallow. Most weather vanes are mounted on hardened steel pivots with agate caps to reduce friction to zero, allowing them to swing at the command of the faintest breath of air. This vane, however, is fitted with a paddle that dips into an annular trough filled with goose lard. It ignores the frantic squalls, the momentary gusts that curl off the cliff faces and signify nothing. It turns only when a wind has blown from the same quarter with the force of an ox-plow for forty uninterrupted minutes. It is a tool for men who do not care about the weather of today, but need to know if the season has broken, if the armada has sailed, or if the winter has finally come down from the pole to stay.

I spend my afternoons between three and five checking the oil in the dashpots and winding the drum-clocks that turn the smoked-paper registers. My hands smell perpetually of neatsfoot oil and old slate. It is not an unhappy life, provided one does not look too long at the horizon through the gap between the headland and the bell-buoy. That gap is four nautical miles across, and on clear days, through the three-inch spyglass, one can see the masts of ships that are hull-down on their way to Bristol or the Plate. They move across the field of view with the smooth, indifferent progress of fat maggots through an apple, their funnels spitting small tufts of brown steam that disperse before they reach the water.

They do not look at the Point. We are not on the Admiralty charts any longer; we were replaced twenty-two years ago by an automated light on an iron skeleton tower six miles further out, on the Shingle Shoal. The Point is merely an anomaly in the coastal survey: *Old stone beacon (disused); radio mast removed.*

***

### III. The Drained Basin

There is an inland sea three days’ walk behind the station, though if you ask the farmers who plant barley in the mud of its former margin, they will tell you it was never a sea at all, but merely the *Grand Marais*.

They lie, but they lie out of thrift. If they admitted it had been an arm of the Atlantic within living memory, the Crown might still claim the rights to the kelp and the wrack-drift, and the titles to their four-acre holdings would turn out to be nothing more than leases held at the pleasure of the Board of Customs.

Fifty years ago, an engineer named Cloutier—a man who had read his Saint-Simon too quickly and whose eyes were set too close together—cut a drainage trench through the basalt bar at Cap-d’Espoir. He had five hundred Irishmen with pickaxes and three stationary steam winches that burned tamarack roots. He promised the syndicate three hundred thousand arpents of black loam that would grow winter wheat for the markets of Montreal.

He got his loam, but the loam was nine-tenths sea-salt and the skeletons of razor-clams. When the water went out, it did not reveal an Arcadia; it revealed a dead, white plain that smelled of rotting sponge and was scored by cracks deep enough to break a pony’s fetlock. The wheat came up three inches high, pale as leek-shoots, turned yellow, and died before the ears could form.

Now, only the samphire grows there, and a low, fleshy shrub with grey leaves that the women call *salt-wood*. In the center of the basin, five miles from the nearest well, lies the *Saint-Malo*, a two-masted brig that was caught in the final ebb when Cloutier’s ditch blew out its cofferdam. She didn't overturn. She settled squarely on her keel into the clay, like a fat hen into her dust-bath. The freshwater rains have washed the pitch from her deck seams, and the frost has opened her topsides so that you can look through her ribs into the dark hold where forty barrels of pickled mackerel have long since turned into grey grease and dry fish-spines.

I walked out to her once, in the second year of my service, carrying a canteen of tea and a notebook.

The seabed under my boots was resilient, like an old mattress stuffed with horsehair. Every few yards, a bubble of gas would burst from the dried crust with a small, flat *pop*, releasing a puff of air that smelled of iron filings and very old weeds. It was an uncanny walk. The sky was high, empty, and uniform—a pale milk-blue that gave no shadow. Without the movement of water, the land seemed to have lost its grain; there was no up or down to it, only a horizon that curved away with terrifying smoothness, broken only by that solitary black hulk standing up like a rotten tooth in an old gum.

When I reached the vessel, I found that someone had climbed up the rudder-irons and carved a name into the transom with a timber-scribe: *J. M. 1888*. Below the name, the carver had not added a verse or a prayer, but a series of twenty-one vertical notches, and then a horizontal bar striking them through.

Twenty-one what? Days spent waiting for the tide to return? Weeks of labor before the salvage was abandoned? Or merely twenty-one bags of ship’s biscuit carried off before the rats got into the bread-room?

There was no answer. The wood was cedar, silvered by the wind and dry as bone. I put my ear against the vessel’s bilge. I wanted to hear the earth, but there was only the hum of the north wind through the empty hawse-holes—a low, reed-organ note that did not change pitch even when the gusts rose.

It is that note which stays with you. A landscape that has had its purpose removed does not revert to nature; it remains an empty theater, waiting for the scenery to be struck, while the light slowly fails and the caretakers go home one by one.

***

### IV. The Mechanics of Neglect

People who do not live alone believe that solitude is an absence. They think it is what happens when you take society away, as if silence were simply the gap between two noises.

It is not. Solitude is a substance. It has weight, density, and a very slow fluid motion, not unlike the pitch that runs down the trunk of a damaged fir. It fills the rooms from the floorboards upward. In my sixth year here, I noticed that the silence had reached the level of the wainscoting; in my twelfth, it was level with the lintels. Now, it is up to the throat of the chimney, and when I speak to myself—which I do only to ensure that the mechanics of the tongue have not rusted like the levers of the psychrometer—the sound does not travel across the room. It falls directly from my lips to the rag-rug, like lead shot dropped into flour.

To keep oneself from dissolving into this substance, one must adopt an aggressive pedantry.

I rise at five. I shave every day, using an English straight-razor that I hone on a strip of horsehide greased with tallow. I use cold water; hot water makes the skin loose and encourages self-pity.

At six, I light the iron stove in the kitchen. I do not burn driftwood; driftwood burns with a spiteful, green flame that leaves a greasy soot on the kettle, and the salt in it eats the fire-bricks out of the stove-back in a single winter. I burn birch, split twelve months before and stacked under the lean-to with the bark-side down so the damp does not get caught in the rolls of paper.

At seven, the readings:
- *Barometer:* 29.84 inches and steady.
- *Thermometer (external):* 4 degrees Celsius.
- *Wind:* East-southeast, force 3, veering slightly toward noon.
- *Precipitation:* None, but the grass is wet with cold dew that has not burned off because the sun is tangled in the hemlocks on the ridge.

After the readings comes the grease.

An archive of iron and brass on an exposed coast is an army under permanent siege. The enemy does not attack with flags; it attacks with an infinite supply of tiny, wet fingers. If I fail to turn the screws of the great sextant on the roof for three weeks, the brass threads will grow together in a cold, metallic marriage called galling. Once galled, no wrench can part them without stripping the tooth; they must be drilled out, and the hole tapped again, and an oversized screw turned down on the small lathe in the tool-shed.

So I go from instrument to instrument with an oil-can made of hammered sheet-copper, its long snout polished bright by forty years of being thrust into narrow spaces. I put a single drop of sperm-oil on each pivot:
- On the escapement of the three-day chronometer by Dent.
- On the knives of the balance-beam that measures the rate of evaporation from an enameled zinc tray.
- On the trunnions of the rain-gauge.
- On the hinge of the weather-vane's tail.

The sperm-oil is old stock, taken from a cask marked *New Bedford, 1869*. It is pale as gin and does not gum, even when the thermometer drops until the mercury clicks in the bulb like a dry pea. It has a smell that I have come to associate with the passage of time itself: not rancid, but animal, ancient, and cool—the fat of a beast that lived forty fathoms down in the dark, preserved now to keep thirty-two little brass wheels turning against each other without screaming.

***

### V. The Visitation

In thirty years, three people have climbed the path from the cove who were not sailors from the supply cutter.

The first was a surveyor from the Department of the Interior who had a map with him that showed a railway line crossing the Point. He was a young man with teeth that were remarkably white, and he wore yellow leather boots that had never been treated with seal-tallow. He spent three days on the rocks with a transit, sighting back toward the spruce-woods and cursing his chain-man, who was a local boy from the church-settlement who smelled of cod-liver.

On the fourth morning, the young man came into the kitchen, sat on my three-legged stool, and looked at his boots, which were now dark grey and had cracked along the welt from the salt-water.

"There is no ballast here," he said.

"No," I told him. "Only the basalt, and that shatters into cubes when you blast it. It has no grain. You cannot lay a road-bed on it."

"The map says it is granite," he said, tapping a finger on his blue-print. His nail was bitten down to the pink.

"The map was made in Ottawa," I replied. "In Ottawa, they think the whole world is granite until you reach the prairies, and then they think it is all butter."

He went away the next day, and three years later the railway company went into liquidation, leaving eight miles of iron track sitting in a spruce-bog twenty miles north, where the moose use the embankment as a dry trail during the spring melts.

The second visitor was a woman. She did not have a notebook or a transit. She had a small basket made of sweetgrass, such as the Micmac girls sell at the ferry-slips, containing six hard-boiled eggs and a pair of dry stockings.

She sat on the bench under the lantern room from ten in the morning until the sun went down behind the ridge. She did not ask for tea, though I went out at noon and set a mug on the stone beside her. She did not drink it. When the shadows of the iron stanchions stretched out across the rocks like long, thin fingers, she stood up, took her stockings out of the basket, put them on over her wet feet, and walked back down the trail toward the cove.

I went out to fetch the mug. The tea was cold, and a small black ant was swimming in the film that had formed on the top. On the grey stone where her skirts had rested, she had left three small white stones from the beach, arranged in an equilateral triangle. I did not touch them. They stayed there until the gale of November fourteenth took them off into the bladderwrack.

The third visitor arrived yesterday.

***

### VI. The Man with the Tin Tube

He did not come by the cove trail. He came along the shore from the south, walking over the seaweed at low water—a thing no one who knows the coast ever does, for the wrack-bladder is greasier than butter on hot iron, and if you slip between the blocks of basalt when the tide is making, you may well drown before anyone hears you yell above the suck of the surge.

He was old, but he had the long, loose-jointed stride of a man who has spent forty years behind a mule. He wore an ulster of greenish tweed that hung to his ankles, and over his shoulder he carried an engineer’s tube of japanned tin with a leather strap.

I watched him through the spyglass from the lantern room. He did not stop to look at the sea. He walked with his head down, watching his boots, his beard—which was yellowish-white and split by the wind into two distinct horns—tucked into the neck of his coat.

When he reached the iron ladder that leads from the kelp-shelf to the platform, he did not call out. He climbed it slowly, using his left hand for the rungs and holding the tin tube against his ribs with his right elbow.

I met him at the kitchen door.

"You have theDent chronometer," he said. His voice was dry, like two sheets of emery paper being rubbed together in a dark room.

"Number 1804," I said. "Three-day movement. Earnshaw balance."

He nodded once, entered the house without scraping his boots, and unslung the tin tube.

He did not take off his coat. He sat down at the pine table, where I had been cleaning the lamp-chimney, took a brass key from his waistcoat pocket, and opened the cap of the cylinder. From it he extracted a single sheet of parchment, perhaps three feet long, which had been rolled so tightly for so long that it resisted being flattened, curling back on itself like a dried salt-cod.

"Hold that corner," he said.

I placed a stone weight—a four-pound lead sinker from the cod-lines—on the north edge, and held the south with the thumb of my left hand.

The sheet was not a map. It was a graph, drawn in two colors of ink: a pale, faded sepia and a very brilliant, venomous green that could only have been copper arsenite. The horizontal axis was marked in years, from 1740 to 1920; the vertical axis was marked in units I did not recognize: *G-zeros*, *minims of deviation*, and *fractions of the fifth degree*.

The sepia line was smooth. It dipped through the middle of the eighteenth century, rose to an apex around the year of the three comets (1811), and then flattened into a long, slow plateau.

The green line was entirely different. It was frantic. It spiked like the heart-trace of a dying dog. It rose through the decades of the coal-iron booms, leaped over the year 1883, and then, around 1905, began to vibrate with such frequency that the ink had run together into a thick, mossy bar that nearly tore through the parchment.

"What is the value?" I asked.

He looked at me with eyes that were watery, small, and completely devoid of interest. They were the eyes of a clerk who has checked invoices for sixty years and no longer cares whether the timber was hemlock or pine, provided the totals in the right-hand column balance to the half-penny.

"The constant," he said.

"Which one?"

"The local one. The weight of the standard pound on this headland."

I smiled. "The pound is sixteen ounces. It does not weigh more or less because it is on a rock in the Gulf."

"It does," he said. He did not raise his voice. He took an ivory rule from his pocket and laid it across the green line at the year 1912. "A pound of lead at Greenwich is sixteen ounces. At the Equator, it is fifteen point nine four, because of the spin. We knew that. Newton knew that. What they did not tell you—what they could not tell you until the deep soundings were run for the telegraph lines—is that the crust is not a floor. It is a skin over cold grease."

He tapped the green line with the horn point of his rule.

"It is thinning here," he said. "The Point is rising. Three millimeters a year since the drainage of the basin. The water had weight. You took the water away, and the stone is coming up like an empty scow after the coal is out. In seven years, the chronometer will run four seconds fast a day, not because the spring is tired, but because you are four hundred feet further from the center of the mass than you were when the light was built."

I looked at the Den chronometer in its mahogany box on the shelf. Its balance was swinging with that calm, circular dignity that has not varied since the year my predecessor died in the wicker armchair with his pipe still between his teeth.

"Does it matter?" I asked.

The old man looked at the corner of the room, where the silence was waiting, level with the shelf.

"Matter to whom?" he asked. "The ships don't use the chronometers now. They have the wireless. They take the time from the mast at Arlington; they take it out of the air like a bird taking a midge. A man in an iron steamer doesn't care if the headland is rising or sinking. He doesn't even care if the headland is there, provided the spark tells him he is five miles south of the banks."

He began to roll up his parchment. It went back into the tube with a dry, rustling hiss, like a snake entering a stone wall.

"Then why did you come?"

He capped the cylinder and turned the brass key until it clicked.

"The Bureau has been closed," he said. "The rooms in the basement at the Department are being given to the Inspector of Fisheries. They told me to burn the sheets."

He stood up. He had not taken off his coat, and he did not ask for a glass of water.

"Did you burn them?"

"I burned the duplicates," he said. "The originals were drawn by my father. He had very good ink. It was made from galls he gathered himself in the oak-openings behind Hamilton. You can't buy that ink now. It has too much acid; it eats the steel pens. Modern pens are too soft for it."

He went down the iron ladder backward, his coat tails blowing around his shins like the wings of a crow that has landed on a dead sheep. When he reached the seaweed, he turned south again, toward the rail-head forty miles away, and I watched him through the spyglass until the green tweed merged with the color of the kelp-shelf and there was only the grey swell rising and falling against the rocks.

***

### VII. The Ledger of Last Instances

It is midnight now.

The wind has gone round to the north, as the *Vane of Uncertain Allegiance* predicted it would twelve hours ago. It is a clean wind, cold as stone from a deep cellar, and it brings no salt with it because it has come over three hundred leagues of spruce forest and muskeg, across the frozen tundra of the Ungava, where the caribou are already standing with their backs to the sleet.

I have not lit the lamp in the lantern room. It is unnecessary. The moon is three days past the full, and the sea has taken on that flat, white shine that makes the rocks look blacker than they are by day.

I sit at the table with the master register—the great folio with the pigskin corners—and I make the final entry for the month of October.

I do not record the surveyor. I do not record the woman with the three stones, nor the man with the green graph. Such things are not terrestrial constants; they are merely the weather of the mind, which passes like the squalls that trouble the surface of the estuary without ever reaching the oysters on the bed.

I record only the values that would be intelligible to the man who sat here in 1860, or to the one who will not come to replace me when I leave:

- *Height of the mercury:* 30.02 inches.
- *Rate of Dent 1804:* Correct.
- *Condition of the light:* Extinguished.
- *State of the coast:* Unchanged.

When the ink is dry, I do not close the book. I leave it open so the parchment does not stick together during the small hours, when the temperature in the stone house drops to the level of the sea outside.

A mile off the Point, the buoy on the Shingle Shoal is whistling. It has an iron lung that is operated by the lift of the sea—a great cylinder that gulps air as the wave falls and drives it through a bronze reed as the crest comes under it. It has whistled like that every seven seconds since I was a boy of twelve, and it will whistle like that until the rivets rust through and the chamber fills with mud, long after the name of Cloutier is forgotten, long after the *Saint-Malo* has rotted down into a little black ridge in the samphire plain, long after the ministry has deleted the last line of the budget that buys the sperm-oil for the pivots.

It is a good sound. It is not an argument. It does not ask whether the earth is rising or falling, or whether the pound in the hand is the pound that was struck in the mint. It merely measures the interval between two waters—an interval that is never quite the same, but which is always, within the error of the instrument, sufficient.

She didn't overturn. She settled squarely on her keel into the clay, like a fat hen into her dust-bath. The freshwater rains have washed the pitch from her deck seams, and the frost has opened her topsides so that you can look through her ribs into the dark hold where forty barrels of pickled mackerel have long since turned into grey grease and dry fish-spines.

I walked out to her once, in the second year of my service, carrying a canteen of tea and a notebook.

The seabed under my boots was resilient, like an old mattress stuffed with horsehair. Every few yards, a bubble of gas would burst from the dried crust with a small, flat *pop*, releasing a puff of air that smelled of iron filings and very old weeds. It was an uncanny walk. The sky was high, empty, and uniform—a pale milk-blue that gave no shadow. Without the movement of water, the land seemed to have lost its grain; there was no up or down to it, only a horizon that curved away with terrifying smoothness, broken only by that solitary black hulk standing up like a rotten tooth in an old gum.

When I reached the vessel, I found that someone had climbed up the rudder-irons and carved a name into the transom with a timber-scribe: *J. M. 1888*. Below the name, the carver had not added a verse or a prayer, but a series of twenty-one vertical notches, and then a horizontal bar striking them through.

Twenty-one what? Days spent waiting for the tide to return? Weeks of labor before the salvage was abandoned? Or merely twenty-one bags of ship’s biscuit carried off before the rats got into the bread-room?

There was no answer. The wood was cedar, silvered by the wind and dry as bone. I put my ear against the vessel’s bilge. I wanted to hear the earth, but there was only the hum of the north wind through the empty hawse-holes—a low, reed-organ note that did not change pitch even when the gusts rose.

It is that note which stays with you. A landscape that has had its purpose removed does not revert to nature; it remains an empty theater, waiting for the scenery to be struck, while the light slowly fails and the caretakers go home one by one.

***

### IV. The Mechanics of Neglect

People who do not live alone believe that solitude is an absence. They think it is what happens when you take society away, as if silence were simply the gap between two noises.

It is not. Solitude is a substance. It has weight, density, and a very slow fluid motion, not unlike the pitch that runs down the trunk of a damaged fir. It fills the rooms from the floorboards upward. In my sixth year here, I noticed that the silence had reached the level of the wainscoting; in my twelfth, it was level with the lintels. Now, it is up to the throat of the chimney, and when I speak to myself—which I do only to ensure that the mechanics of the tongue have not rusted like the levers of the psychrometer—the sound does not travel across the room. It falls directly from my lips to the rag-rug, like lead shot dropped into flour.

To keep oneself from dissolving into this substance, one must adopt an aggressive pedantry.

I rise at five. I shave every day, using an English straight-razor that I hone on a strip of horsehide greased with tallow. I use cold water; hot water makes the skin loose and encourages self-pity.

At six, I light the iron stove in the kitchen. I do not burn driftwood; driftwood burns with a spiteful, green flame that leaves a greasy soot on the kettle, and the salt in it eats the fire-bricks out of the stove-back in a single winter. I burn birch, split twelve months before and stacked under the lean-to with the bark-side down so the damp does not get caught in the rolls of paper.

At seven, the readings:
- *Barometer:* 29.84 inches and steady.
- *Thermometer (external):* 4 degrees Celsius.
- *Wind:* East-southeast, force 3, veering slightly toward noon.
- *Precipitation:* None, but the grass is wet with cold dew that has not burned off because the sun is tangled in the hemlocks on the ridge.

After the readings comes the grease.

An archive of iron and brass on an exposed coast is an army under permanent siege. The enemy does not attack with flags; it attacks with an infinite supply of tiny, wet fingers. If I fail to turn the screws of the great sextant on the roof for three weeks, the brass threads will grow together in a cold, metallic marriage called galling. Once galled, no wrench can part them without stripping the tooth; they must be drilled out, and the hole tapped again, and an oversized screw turned down on the small lathe in the tool-shed.

So I go from instrument to instrument with an oil-can made of hammered sheet-copper, its long snout polished bright by forty years of being thrust into narrow spaces. I put a single drop of sperm-oil on each pivot:
- On the escapement of the three-day chronometer by Dent.
- On the knives of the balance-beam that measures the rate of evaporation from an enameled zinc tray.
- On the trunnions of the rain-gauge.
- On the hinge of the weather-vane's tail.

The sperm-oil is old stock, taken from a cask marked *New Bedford, 1869*. It is pale as gin and does not gum, even when the thermometer drops until the mercury clicks in the bulb like a dry pea. It has a smell that I have come to associate with the passage of time itself: not rancid, but animal, ancient, and cool—the fat of a beast that lived forty fathoms down in the dark, preserved now to keep thirty-two little brass wheels turning against each other without screaming.

***

### V. The Visitation

In thirty years, three people have climbed the path from the cove who were not sailors from the supply cutter.

The first was a surveyor from the Department of the Interior who had a map with him that showed a railway line crossing the Point. He was a young man with teeth that were remarkably white, and he wore yellow leather boots that had never been treated with seal-tallow. He spent three days on the rocks with a transit, sighting back toward the spruce-woods and cursing his chain-man, who was a local boy from the church-settlement who smelled of cod-liver.

On the fourth morning, the young man came into the kitchen, sat on my three-legged stool, and looked at his boots, which were now dark grey and had cracked along the welt from the salt-water.

"There is no ballast here," he said.

"No," I told him. "Only the basalt, and that shatters into cubes when you blast it. It has no grain. You cannot lay a road-bed on it."

"The map says it is granite," he said, tapping a finger on his blue-print. His nail was bitten down to the pink.

"The map was made in Ottawa," I replied. "In Ottawa, they think the whole world is granite until you reach the prairies, and then they think it is all butter."

He went away the next day, and three years later the railway company went into liquidation, leaving eight miles of iron track sitting in a spruce-bog twenty miles north, where the moose use the embankment as a dry trail during the spring melts.

The second visitor was a woman. She did not have a notebook or a transit. She had a small basket made of sweetgrass, such as the Micmac girls sell at the ferry-slips, containing six hard-boiled eggs and a pair of dry stockings.

She sat on the bench under the lantern room from ten in the morning until the sun went down behind the ridge. She did not ask for tea, though I went out at noon and set a mug on the stone beside her. She did not drink it. When the shadows of the iron stanchions stretched out across the rocks like long, thin fingers, she stood up, took her stockings out of the basket, put them on over her wet feet, and walked back down the trail toward the cove.

I went out to fetch the mug. The tea was cold, and a small black ant was swimming in the film that had formed on the top. On the grey stone where her skirts had rested, she had left three small white stones from the beach, arranged in an equilateral triangle. I did not touch them. They stayed there until the gale of November fourteenth took them off into the bladderwrack.

The third visitor arrived yesterday.

***

### VI. The Man with the Tin Tube

He did not come by the cove trail. He came along the shore from the south, walking over the seaweed at low water—a thing no one who knows the coast ever does, for the wrack-bladder is greasier than butter on hot iron, and if you slip between the blocks of basalt when the tide is making, you may well drown before anyone hears you yell above the suck of the surge.

He was old, but he had the long, loose-jointed stride of a man who has spent forty years behind a mule. He wore an ulster of greenish tweed that hung to his ankles, and over his shoulder he carried an engineer’s tube of japanned tin with a leather strap.

I watched him through the spyglass from the lantern room. He did not stop to look at the sea. He walked with his head down, watching his boots, his beard—which was yellowish-white and split by the wind into two distinct horns—tucked into the neck of his coat.

When he reached the iron ladder that leads from the kelp-shelf to the platform, he did not call out. He climbed it slowly, using his left hand for the rungs and holding the tin tube against his ribs with his right elbow.

I met him at the kitchen door.

"You have theDent chronometer," he said. His voice was dry, like two sheets of emery paper being rubbed together in a dark room.

"Number 1804," I said. "Three-day movement. Earnshaw balance."

He nodded once, entered the house without scraping his boots, and unslung the tin tube.

He did not take off his coat. He sat down at the pine table, where I had been cleaning the lamp-chimney, took a brass key from his waistcoat pocket, and opened the cap of the cylinder. From it he extracted a single sheet of parchment, perhaps three feet long, which had been rolled so tightly for so long that it resisted being flattened, curling back on itself like a dried salt-cod.

"Hold that corner," he said.

I placed a stone weight—a four-pound lead sinker from the cod-lines—on the north edge, and held the south with the thumb of my left hand.

The sheet was not a map. It was a graph, drawn in two colors of ink: a pale, faded sepia and a very brilliant, venomous green that could only have been copper arsenite. The horizontal axis was marked in years, from 1740 to 1920; the vertical axis was marked in units I did not recognize: *G-zeros*, *minims of deviation*, and *fractions of the fifth degree*.

The sepia line was smooth. It dipped through the middle of the eighteenth century, rose to an apex around the year of the three comets (1811), and then flattened into a long, slow plateau.

The green line was entirely different. It was frantic. It spiked like the heart-trace of a dying dog. It rose through the decades of the coal-iron booms, leaped over the year 1883, and then, around 1905, began to vibrate with such frequency that the ink had run together into a thick, mossy bar that nearly tore through the parchment.

"What is the value?" I asked.

He looked at me with eyes that were watery, small, and completely devoid of interest. They were the eyes of a clerk who has checked invoices for sixty years and no longer cares whether the timber was hemlock or pine, provided the totals in the right-hand column balance to the half-penny.

"The constant," he said.

"Which one?"

"The local one. The weight of the standard pound on this headland."

I smiled. "The pound is sixteen ounces. It does not weigh more or less because it is on a rock in the Gulf."

"It does," he said. He did not raise his voice. He took an ivory rule from his pocket and laid it across the green line at the year 1912. "A pound of lead at Greenwich is sixteen ounces. At the Equator, it is fifteen point nine four, because of the spin. We knew that. Newton knew that. What they did not tell you—what they could not tell you until the deep soundings were run for the telegraph lines—is that the crust is not a floor. It is a skin over cold grease."

He tapped the green line with the horn point of his rule.

"It is thinning here," he said. "The Point is rising. Three millimeters a year since the drainage of the basin. The water had weight. You took the water away, and the stone is coming up like an empty scow after the coal is out. In seven years, the chronometer will run four seconds fast a day, not because the spring is tired, but because you are four hundred feet further from the center of the mass than you were when the light was built."

I looked at the Den chronometer in its mahogany box on the shelf. Its balance was swinging with that calm, circular dignity that has not varied since the year my predecessor died in the wicker armchair with his pipe still between his teeth.

"Does it matter?" I asked.

The old man looked at the corner of the room, where the silence was waiting, level with the shelf.

"Matter to whom?" he asked. "The ships don't use the chronometers now. They have the wireless. They take the time from the mast at Arlington; they take it out of the air like a bird taking a midge. A man in an iron steamer doesn't care if the headland is rising or sinking. He doesn't even care if the headland is there, provided the spark tells him he is five miles south of the banks."

He began to roll up his parchment. It went back into the tube with a dry, rustling hiss, like a snake entering a stone wall.

"Then why did you come?"

He capped the cylinder and turned the brass key until it clicked.

"The Bureau has been closed," he said. "The rooms in the basement at the Department are being given to the Inspector of Fisheries. They told me to burn the sheets."

He stood up. He had not taken off his coat, and he did not ask for a glass of water.

"Did you burn them?"

"I burned the duplicates," he said. "The originals were drawn by my father. He had very good ink. It was made from galls he gathered himself in the oak-openings behind Hamilton. You can't buy that ink now. It has too much acid; it eats the steel pens. Modern pens are too soft for it."

He went down the iron ladder backward, his coat tails blowing around his shins like the wings of a crow that has landed on a dead sheep. When he reached the seaweed, he turned south again, toward the rail-head forty miles away, and I watched him through the spyglass until the green tweed merged with the color of the kelp-shelf and there was only the grey swell rising and falling against the rocks.

***

### VII. The Ledger of Last Instances

It is midnight now.

The wind has gone round to the north, as the *Vane of Uncertain Allegiance* predicted it would twelve hours ago. It is a clean wind, cold as stone from a deep cellar, and it brings no salt with it because it has come over three hundred leagues of spruce forest and muskeg, across the frozen tundra of the Ungava, where the caribou are already standing with their backs to the sleet.

I have not lit the lamp in the lantern room. It is unnecessary. The moon is three days past the full, and the sea has taken on that flat, white shine that makes the rocks look blacker than they are by day.

I sit at the table with the master register—the great folio with the pigskin corners—and I make the final entry for the month of October.

I do not record the surveyor. I do not record the woman with the three stones, nor the man with the green graph. Such things are not terrestrial constants; they are merely the weather of the mind, which passes like the squalls that trouble the surface of the estuary without ever reaching the oysters on the bed.

I record only the values that would be intelligible to the man who sat here in 1860, or to the one who will not come to replace me when I leave:

- *Height of the mercury:* 30.02 inches.
- *Rate of Dent 1804:* Correct.
- *Condition of the light:* Extinguished.
- *State of the coast:* Unchanged.

When the ink is dry, I do not close the book. I leave it open so the parchment does not stick together during the small hours, when the temperature in the stone house drops to the level of the sea outside.

A mile off the Point, the buoy on the Shingle Shoal is whistling. It has an iron lung that is operated by the lift of the sea—a great cylinder that gulps air as the wave falls and drives it through a bronze reed as the crest comes under it. It has whistled like that every seven seconds since I was a boy of twelve, and it will whistle like that until the rivets rust through and the chamber fills with mud, long after the name of Cloutier is forgotten, long after the *Saint-Malo* has rotted down into a little black ridge in the samphire plain, long after the ministry has deleted the last line of the budget that buys the sperm-oil for the pivots.

It is a good sound. It is not an argument. It does not ask whether the earth is rising or falling, or whether the pound in the hand is the pound that was struck in the mint. It merely measures the interval between two waters—an interval that is never quite the same, but which is always, within the error of the instrument, sufficient.
